clips.title: Module Bundlers Explained... Webpack, Rollup, Parcel, and Snowpack
clips.why: Why bundlers exist at all, and what one does with your imports, in two minutes.
look: The problem: code spread over many files and packages.
What a module bundler does: follow the imports and produce one output.
clips.after: esbuild does this for the harness, so Nova's machine gets one file instead of a node_modules folder.

clips.title: How to bundle a nodejs lambda function? (using esbuild)
clips.why: The same problem as ours on AWS Lambda: ship Node code with its npm dependencies to a machine that will not install them.
look: Bundling a function together with its npm dependencies.
Looking at the bundle's size to see which packages are inside it.
clips.after: Nova's machine is like the Lambda here: it gets one tested file, and the bundle carries zod, yaml and the rest inside.

clips.title: what is a shebang (#!)? (beginner - intermediate) anthony explains #033
clips.why: A clear explanation of the first line of our bundle: how the operating system decides which program runs a script.
look: What #! on the first line tells the operating system.
Why the file must also be executable (chmod +x).
clips.after: With #!/usr/bin/env node and chmod +x, the image can link /usr/local/bin/nova-worker straight to the bundle.

practice.q: Why does tsc's dist/ output fail on a machine with no node_modules?

options.text: tsc only translates your own files; every package import stays an import that Node must find
options.why: A bundler follows those imports into node_modules and puts the code in the file. tsc does not.
With NodeNext and "type": "module" it writes ES modules. The problem is the missing packages.

options.text: The files need TypeScript installed to run
options.why: dist/ is plain JavaScript. Node runs it without TypeScript.

practice.q: Tell esbuild to pull every import, packages included, into the output file.
practice.hint: One word: what you want to make.
practice.why: Without --bundle, esbuild only translates the one file, like tsc, and zod stays an import.

practice.q: The first line of the bundle that lets the operating system run it with node.
practice.hint: A shebang: hash, exclamation mark, then the env program and the name of the runtime.
practice.why: With this line and chmod +x, ./lab-worker.mjs works like any command, which is how /usr/local/bin/nova-worker is linked.

practice.q: A bundle builds cleanly but fails when it runs with Dynamic require of "process" is not supported. What fixes it?

options.why: It was already there; the build would have complained about node: imports otherwise.

options.text: A banner line that creates require with createRequire(import.meta.url)
options.why: A CommonJS package inside the ES module bundle calls require, which does not exist there. The banner gives it a real one.

options.text: Switch to --format=cjs and keep the .mjs ending
options.why: A .mjs file is always read as an ES module, so CommonJS output in it breaks differently.

practice.q: Put the path of the harness from source to Nova's machine in order.
items: esbuild bundles harness/ into nova-worker.mjs with a shebang
The bundle is run from an empty folder to prove nothing is missing
The release job packs it into a .tgz and attaches it to a GitHub release
The image build downloads the asset and unpacks it
/usr/local/bin/nova-worker points at the file, with nothing installed
practice.why: One tested file travels unchanged from the build to the machine, and the same file runs in the benchmark.
